title: Protocol to Evaluate Human Thermoregulation Before and After Thermal Stress
author: Castrillón-Gutiérrez, Olaya-Mira, et al.
materials: Welch Allyn SureTemp® Plus 690 electronic thermometer

The protocol was designed considering clinical, environmental, and technical factors and ensuring its reproducibility in both healthy and pathological populations. Thermographic images were acquired both at rest and after thermal stress (modified Bruce test). In addition, questionnaires were prepared to collect and store information on demographic data, core temperature, environmental conditions, pain perception, and level of physical activity.

Core body temperature should be measured orally using an electronic thermometer with a minimum accuracy of ± 0.1 °C. Environmental conditions should be monitored with a digital thermohygrometer with an accuracy of ± 1 °C.

Since this protocol involves physical activity to induce thermal stress, participants are classified based on their level of activity (Sedentary, Lightly Active, Moderately Active, or Active), as this could be a key factor in thermoregulatory behavior. Therefore, to assess physical activity, this protocol includes items from the Rapid Assessment of Physical Activity (RAPA) questionnaire [11], as well as questions about the duration, intensity, and flexibility of said activity (see supplementary material).

The upper-body images capture the area from the forehead to the iliac crests, while the lower-body images cover the region from the inguinal groove to the soles of the feet. The thermograms acquired in S1 and S2 are processed to find the average temperature of the body areas captured in each image.

To process the images in MATLAB, the thermograms should be saved in MAT file format using the structure shown in Fig. 3. The algorithm reads the images; removes background noise, retaining only the pixel information associated with the participant's body; and then applies first-order statistical texture analysis. This analysis calculates up to six texture measurements, including the average temperature, which is derived from the grey levels of the body surface pixels in each IRT image. Therefore, the data processing yields twelve average temperatures, corresponding to the twelve images of each participant and stage.

steps.title: Prepare measurement environment
steps.instruction: Set up a measurement area of at least 2 × 3 m. Maintain ambient temperature between 18 °C and 25 °C and relative humidity between 40 % and 70 %. Turn off all lights and cover windows to eliminate infrared interference. Remove external air currents, heating pipes, and exposed electrical wiring. Install a dark backdrop and place a platform for the participant so the camera can be positioned perpendicular to the lower limbs.

steps.title: Set up thermal imaging camera
steps.instruction: Use a camera with minimum 320 × 240 focal‑plane array, wavelength range 8–12 µm, temperature range 20 °C–120 °C, maximum focal length 2.5 m, measurement traceability ≤2 % of reading, and NETD <30 mK. Ensure current calibration. Mount the camera on a tripod, level it, and position it approximately 2 m from the target, keeping the optical axis perpendicular (90°) to the body region. Align the camera parallel to the area of interest for all images and set skin emissivity to 0.98 (either on‑camera or during processing). Use markers to maintain the 2 m distance.

steps.title: Calibrate equipment
steps.instruction: Calibrate the thermal camera, the oral electronic thermometer (accuracy ±0.1 °C), and the digital thermohygrometer (accuracy ±1 °C) according to each manufacturer’s recommendations before any measurements.

steps.title: Screen and record participants
steps.instruction: Define inclusion and exclusion criteria for the study population and include a healthy control group. For each candidate, collect gender, age, weight, height, presence of recent lesions, scars, tattoos, diseases, pain, disabilities, and Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score using the Physiological Selection and Characterization (PSC) questionnaire. Store responses in an Excel spreadsheet with conditional formulas to determine eligibility.

steps.title: Assess activity level
steps.instruction: Classify participants’ habitual physical activity (Sedentary, Lightly Active, Moderately Active, Active) using items from the Rapid Assessment of Physical Activity (RAPA) questionnaire and additional questions on duration, intensity, and flexibility of activity.

steps.title: Give pre‑test participant instructions
steps.instruction: Instruct participants to avoid intense physical activity for 12 h before the test, and to refrain from coffee, alcohol, energy drinks, and nicotine for 3 h before testing. Ensure no creams, lotions, or oils are applied on the skin at the time of imaging. Schedule measurements in the morning to minimise metabolic variability.

steps.title: Complete pre‑imaging pain questionnaire
steps.instruction: Have participants fill out the Pain Perception Questionnaire (PPQ) before any imaging. The PPQ includes four body illustrations (posterior, anterior, left, right) with pain ratings from 1–10, space for comments, and fields to record core body temperature, ambient temperature, and relative humidity. Store the completed forms in the study database.

steps.title: Acclimate and position participants
steps.instruction: Allow participants to rest for 10–15 min to reach thermal equilibrium. Then have them stand on the platform in front of the dark backdrop and assume the positions described in Table 1 (upper‑body: forehead to iliac crests; lower‑body: inguinal groove to soles). Use markers to ensure consistent stance.

steps.title: Acquire baseline thermograms
steps.instruction: Capture infrared thermographic (IRT) images (stage S1) of the upper and lower body using the camera settings described above (2 m distance, emissivity 0.98). Follow the twelve positional views listed in Table 1 for full‑body coverage.

steps.title: Record baseline heart rate
steps.instruction: Measure each participant’s resting heart rate (HR) immediately after the S1 image set.

steps.title: Conduct modified Bruce test
Record exertion after each stage
steps.instruction: After each treadmill stage, have the participant complete the Physical Activity Response (PAR) questionnaire, noting the measured HR and perceived exertion using the Borg scale (0–10).

steps.title: Complete post‑activity pain questionnaire
steps.instruction: Immediately after the treadmill test, ask participants to fill out the PPQ again, recording any changes in pain perception.

steps.title: Acquire post‑activity thermograms
steps.instruction: Capture the second set of IRT images (stage S2) using the identical camera settings, distance, emissivity, and participant positions as for S1.

steps.title: Organize image files
steps.instruction: Create a folder for each participant named with a code beginning with “P” followed by a sequential number (e.g., P1, P2). Inside each participant folder, create subfolders “S1” and “S2” to store the pre‑ and post‑activity images respectively.

steps.title: Convert images to analysis format
steps.instruction: Convert the acquired images to MATLAB‑compatible formats such as .MAT, .CSV, or matrix files as required for downstream processing.

steps.title: Process thermograms in MATLAB
steps.instruction: Load each MAT file, remove background noise to retain only body pixels, and apply first‑order statistical texture analysis. Compute up to six texture metrics, including the average temperature derived from grey‑level values. This yields twelve average temperatures per participant per stage (one for each of the twelve positional images).
